title: The hands and the breath of God
source_text: Ἐγκαλεῖ δ᾿ ἡμῖν ὡς ὑπὸ χειρῶν θεοῦ πλασθέντα εἰσαγαγοῦσιν ἄνθρωπον. τοῦ μὲν τῆς Γενέσεως βιβλίου οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῆς ποιήσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὔτ᾿ ἐπὶ τῆς πλάσεως χεῖρας παραλαβόντος θεοῦ. τοῦ δὲ Ἰὼβ καὶ τοῦ Δαυὶδ εἰπόντων τό· „αἱ χεῖρές σου ἐποίησάν με καὶ ἔπλασάν με,“ περὶ ὧν „πολὺς“ „ὁ λόγος“ εἰς τὸ παραστῆσαι τὰ νενοημένα τοῖς ταῦτα εἰρηκόσιν οὐ μόνον περὶ διαφορᾶς ποιήσεως καὶ πλάσεως ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ χειρῶν θεοῦ· ἃς οἱ μὴ νοήσαντες καὶ τὰς τοιαύτας ἀπὸ τῶν θείων γραφῶν φωνὰς οἴονται ἡμᾶς τοιοῦτον σχῆμα περιτιθέναι τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ ὁποῖόν ἐστι τὸ ἀνθρώπινον, καθ᾿ οὓς καὶ πτέρυγας ἀκόλουθον νομίζειν ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἐν τῷ σώματι τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐπεὶ καὶ ταῦτα λέγουσιν αἱ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν γραφαί. ταῦτα δὲ νῦν ἑρμηνεύειν οὐκ ἀπαιτεῖ ἡ προκειμένη πραγματεία· προηγουμένως γὰρ ἐν τοῖς εἰς τὴν Γένεσιν ἐξηγητικοῖς ταῦθ᾿ ἡμῖν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐξήτασται. εἶθ᾿ ὅρα κακοήθειαν τοῦ Κέλσου ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς. τῆς γὰρ γραφῆς ἡμῶν λεγούσης ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου πλάσεως· „καὶ ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν ζωῆς. καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν,“ ὁ δὲ κακοήθως διασύρειν βουλόμενος τὸ „ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν (ζωῆς) ,“ ὅπερ οὐδὲ νενόηκε τίνα τρόπον λέλεκται, ἀνέγραψεν ὅτι συνέθεσαν ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ χειρῶν θεοῦ πλασσόμενον (καὶ ἐμφυσώμενον) , ἵνα τὸ ἐμφυσώμενον παραπλησίως τις νομίσας λελέχθαι τοῖς ἐμφυσωμένοις ἀσκοῖς γελάσῃ τὸ „ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν ζωῆς“ τροπικῶς εἰρημένον καὶ δεόμενον διηγήσεως, παριστάσης μεταδεδωκέναι τὸν θεὸν τοῦ ἀφθάρτου πνεύματος τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ· καθὸ λέλεκται· „τὸ δὲ ἄφθαρτόν σου πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἐν πᾶσιν.“
pass_a_gloss: He charges (ἐγκαλεῖ) us as introducing (εἰσαγαγοῦσιν) a man moulded (πλασθέντα) by hands of God, the book of Genesis having taken up (παραλαβόντος) hands of God neither at the making (ποιήσεως) of man nor at the moulding (πλάσεως); but Job and David having said: 'your hands made (ἐποίησαν) me and moulded (ἔπλασαν) me', about which 'much [is] the word' (πολὺς ὁ λόγος) to present the things meant (νενοημένα) by those who said them, not only about the difference (διαφορᾶς) of making and moulding but also about hands of God; which those not understanding, and such expressions (φωνάς) from the divine writings, think we attribute (περιτιθέναι) to the God over all (τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ) such a shape (σχῆμα) as is the human; according to whom it is consequent (ἀκόλουθον) that we think there are also wings (πτέρυγας) on the body of God, since the writings about our God according to the letter (κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν) say these too. To interpret (ἑρμηνεύειν) these now the present treatise (πραγματεία) does not demand; for principally (προηγουμένως) in the exegetical [works] (ἐξηγητικοῖς) on Genesis these have been examined (ἐξήτασται) by us as far as possible. Then see the malice (κακοήθειαν) of Celsus in what follows. For our writing saying at the moulding of man: 'and he breathed into (ἐνεφύσησεν) his face (πρόσωπον) breath of life (πνοὴν ζωῆς), and the man became a living soul (ψυχὴν ζῶσαν)', he, wishing maliciously to disparage (διασύρειν) 'he breathed into his face breath [of life]', which he did not even understand in what manner it was said, wrote that they composed a man moulded by hands of God [and blown into (ἐμφυσώμενον)], so that someone, thinking 'blown into' said similarly to blown-up wineskins (ἐμφυσωμένοις ἀσκοῖς), would laugh at 'he breathed into his face breath of life', said figuratively (τροπικῶς) and needing explanation (διηγήσεως), [an explanation] showing that God imparted (μεταδεδωκέναι) [a share] of the incorruptible spirit (ἀφθάρτου πνεύματος) to man; as it is said: 'and your incorruptible spirit is in all things'.
pass_b_english: He charges us with bringing in a man moulded by the hands of God, although the book of Genesis speaks of God’s hands neither at the making of man (Genesis 1:26–27) nor at his moulding (Genesis 2:7). It is Job and David who said, “Your hands made me and moulded me” (Job 10:8; Psalm 119:73). On these words “there is much to say” (Hebrews 5:11) in order to bring out what those who spoke them meant, not only about the difference between making and moulding but also about the hands of God.

Those who have not understood these hands, or similar expressions of the divine Scriptures, think that we ascribe to the God over all a shape such as the human shape. On their reasoning it would follow that we also think there are wings on God’s body, since the Scriptures about our God, taken literally, say this too (see Psalm 17:8; 91:4). But the present treatise does not require us to explain these things now; for we have examined them as our main subject, as far as we could, in our commentaries on Genesis.

Next, see Celsus’s malice in what follows. Our Scripture says of the moulding of man: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). But he, wishing maliciously to mock “he breathed into his face the breath of life”, though he has not even understood in what sense it was said, wrote that they put together “a man moulded by the hands of God and blown into”. He did this so that someone might suppose “blown into” was said in the way wineskins are blown up, and laugh at “he breathed into his face the breath of life”. Yet this was said figuratively and needs an explanation, one showing that God gave man a share of the incorruptible Spirit, as it is said: “Your incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1).

choices.choice: 'Those who have not understood these and similar expressions' -> 'Those who have not understood these hands, or similar expressions' (ἃς is feminine and refers to χεῖρας, not to φωνάς)

Checked: Job 10:8 (LXX verbs reversed) and Psalm 119:73 (= LXX 118:73, exact wording); Hebrews 5:11 (πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος); Psalm 17:8 (= LXX 16:8) and 91:4 (= LXX 90:4) for God's wings; Genesis 1:26-27 and 2:7 (LXX 'into his face'); Wisdom of Solomon 12:1; all kept
Celsus's quoted words ('a man moulded by the hands of God and blown into') match 4.36; speaker frames ('he charges us', 'he wrote') kept as in the Greek

'Your hands made me and moulded me': the wording matches LXX Psalm 118:73 exactly (αἱ χεῖρές σου ἐποίησάν με καὶ ἔπλασάν με) = English Psalm 119:73; LXX Job 10:8 has the verbs in reverse order (ἔπλασάν με καὶ ἐποίησάν με). 'πολὺς ὁ λόγος' is set in quotation marks in the staged text as an echo of Hebrews 5:11 (περὶ οὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος). Making (ποίησις) vs moulding (πλάσις) refers to Genesis 1:26–27 (ποιήσωμεν, ἐποίησεν) and Genesis 2:7 (ἔπλασεν). The wings of God are a general allusion; examples given are LXX Psalm 16:8 = English 17:8 and LXX Psalm 90:4 = English 91:4 (both 'wings' of God). Genesis 2:7 is quoted from the LXX, which has 'into his face' (εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον), kept here instead of the Hebrew-based 'nostrils'. Celsus's 'ἐμφυσώμενον' rendered 'blown into' and the wineskins 'blown up', to keep Origen's point that Celsus chose wording that invites the image of an inflated skin; the bracketed supplements (ζωῆς) and (καὶ ἐμφυσώμενον) in the staged text are editorial and accepted. Wisdom 12:1 LXX reads 'τὸ γὰρ ἄφθαρτόν σου πνεῦμα'; Origen's text has δέ; the particle is left untranslated. 'Spirit' is capitalised because Wisdom 12:1 speaks of God's own spirit and Origen reads the inbreathing as a share in it; a reviewer may prefer lower case for 'the incorruptible spirit' in Origen's own clause. Origen's lost commentaries on Genesis are the 'exegetical works' referred to. Reviewer: ἃς in 'ἃς οἱ μὴ νοήσαντες' is feminine and refers to the hands (χεῖρας), so 'these hands' is made explicit; capital 'Spirit' kept, since Origen reads Wisdom 12:1 of God's own Spirit given to man.
